title: First exchange
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: This course speaks Sie, and this is the rung where that starts to show. Sie is not a politeness coating on a familiar verb: it is its own grammatical person and it takes the PLURAL verb form — Sie sind, Sie kommen, Sie heißen, Sie sprechen — with its own possessive Ihr and its own dative Ihnen. German also has a familiar du with a second set of endings and its own dein, dich and dir; choosing between them is a later level's work, and nothing here is written with it.

German greets by the clock rather than by the room: Guten Morgen early, Guten Tag from mid-morning until the evening, Guten Abend after that. Guten Tag is the safe one with a stranger. Hallo is the friendly version that belongs with du — you will hear it all day and this course never writes it — and the matching goodbye is Auf Wiedersehen, not the Tschüss a friend would use.

A yes/no question is VERB-FIRST, and nothing at all is inserted: the statement Sie sind müde becomes the question Sind Sie müde? by moving the verb to the front. The same single move works on every German verb — Kommen Sie aus Indien?, Sprechen Sie Deutsch?

There is no German word standing in for English "do". The question does not build one and the negative does not either, so a learner hunting for the German "do" is hunting for a word that does not exist. Tun Sie müde sein? is not a near miss — it is a sentence with two verbs and no grammar.

Wellbeing puts the PERSON in a case slot and a meaningless es in the subject slot: Wie geht es Ihnen? is "how goes it to-you", and Mir geht es gut is "to-me goes it well". English does the opposite — it makes the person the subject — so this shape has to be learned whole. It is a pattern German reuses: a later rung says Mir ist kalt for "I'm cold".

nicht is the general "not". It negates a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence and it stands AFTER the verb, or at the end of the clause: Ich bin nicht müde, Ich wohne nicht in Berlin. German has a second "not" for negating a noun, which a later rung teaches, so nicht is not the answer to every English "not".

doch is a yes English has no word for: the yes that CONTRADICTS a negative question. Asked Sind Sie nicht müde? — "aren't you tired?" — ja agrees with the not and says you are not tired. Doch pushes back and means "yes, I am".

One spelling, three readings, and only the verb and the capital separate them. Capitalised mid-sentence, Sie is the formal "you" and takes a plural verb: Sie sind. Lowercase sie with a singular verb is "she": sie ist müde. Lowercase sie with a plural verb is "they": sie sind müde. And because every German noun has a gender, that same lowercase sie also stands for a feminine THING where English says "it".
ja and nein do exactly what "yes" and "no" do, and like English they are answers rather than parts of the sentence: a comma follows, and then a whole ordinary statement.

An adjective after sein takes no ending at all, exactly as in English: Ich bin müde, Sie sind müde, Anna ist müde — one shape for every person. Endings only appear on an adjective standing in front of a noun, which this level keeps out of the way.

words.note: The safe all-day greeting for a stranger; Guten Morgen early, Guten Abend after dark. Take it as one piece. Hallo belongs with du, so this course never writes it.
Frau is the noun “woman” (die Frau) and the title before a surname: Frau Weber; Herr is the male one. On Sie terms you use Herr/Frau + SURNAME, never the first name.
A common German surname. Surnames carry over unchanged, take a capital like every German noun, and are what follows Frau or Herr — Frau Weber, Herr Weber. Swap in whichever one you actually need.

sentences.trap: English greets by the room and the mood — "hi", "hello", "morning" — and then reaches straight for a first name. German greets by the clock, and while you are on Sie terms the name that follows is Herr or Frau plus a SURNAME. Guten Tag, Anna is not a warmer version of this line; it is a different relationship.
sentences.sound: GOO-ten TAHK, frow VAY-ber. The final g of Tag hardens to a k, exactly as it did in mag. Frau has the ow of English "how", and Weber begins with a v, because German w always does.

variations.changed: the clock moves back: this is the greeting before about eleven
the clock moves forward: this one takes over from about six
Herr for a man where Frau was for a woman — and a surname after it either way

mistake.why: The -n is not optional. The greeting is a frozen phrase and it is always Guten Tag, Guten Morgen, Guten Abend — the ending is carrying grammar this level does not otherwise need, which is exactly why the phrase is learned whole.

sentences.usage: The first thing you say walking into a shop, an office or a waiting room, and the one greeting that is safe with anyone at any hour of the working day.
sentences.mnemonic: "Good day" with the words in the English order. The only two things to hold are the -n on Guten and the fact that German greets by the clock.

words.note: how — here doing English's “what”: German asks HOW you are called, not what your name is. The same wie opens Wie geht es Ihnen? and later asks quantity.
One word, three meanings — read the CAPITAL and the VERB. Capital Sie + plural verb is formal “you” (Sie sind). Lowercase sie + singular verb is “she”; + plural verb is “they”.

sentences.trap: English asks WHAT your name is. German asks HOW you are called, and the verb it uses is the one from the last rung — heißen. Translating the English question word for word gives you a sentence a German speaker has to decode.
sentences.sound: vee HIGH-sen zee. w is v, so wie begins with a v sound; ie is read by its second letter, so it comes out "ee". A single s in front of a vowel is voiced like an English z, which is why Sie is "zee" — while the ß in heißen stays a sharp, unvoiced s.

variations.changed: the same verb turned back on yourself — the question's -en ending becomes -e for ich
the same question built out of a noun instead of a verb — the form a counter or an official will use
an open question becomes a yes/no one: the question word goes and the verb takes the front

mistake.why: After a question word the verb comes straight away, before the subject: Wie heißen Sie? Leaving the verb behind the subject is the English order, and in German it is the shape a subordinate clause takes — on its own it is not a question at all.

sentences.usage: How you ask a stranger's name: at a desk, on the phone, at a door. With a friend the same question uses du and a different ending, which a later level teaches.
sentences.mnemonic: German asks HOW, not what: wie heißen Sie — how are you called.

words.note: The possessive of Sie: Ihr Name. Capitalised like Sie — the capital alone separates it from ihr (“her/their”), not taught here. Bare before a masculine or neuter noun, like ein.
Name — der Name, capitalised. Behind Wie ist Ihr Name?, the form's and the counter's question; the spoken one is Wie heißen Sie? On Sie terms the answer is the surname.

sentences.trap: There is nothing to insert and nothing to shuffle: the statement Ihr Name ist Anna becomes a question by moving ist to the front. English needs "is" to move too here — the delta is that German does this with every verb it has, and never borrows a "do".
sentences.sound: ist eer NAH-muh VAY-ber. Ihr is a long "ee" and the h is silent — an h after a vowel is there to lengthen it, never to be pronounced. Name has two syllables, NAH-muh, ending in that unstressed "uh" German gives every final -e.

variations.changed: the same four words as a statement — the question was only ist moving to the front
swap the name being checked; nothing else in the frame moves
a yes/no question becomes an open one: the question word takes the front and the verb stays in second place behind it

mistake.why: Name is masculine — der Name — so the possessive stays bare: Ihr Name. The -e is the feminine ending, the same one that turns ein into eine, and it does not belong here.

sentences.usage: What a receptionist, a delivery driver or an official asks when they are checking they have the right person.
sentences.mnemonic: Ihr Name — two capitals, and each one is earned: the possessive that goes with Sie keeps its capital, and every German noun keeps its own.

words.note: Yes, as in English — with one gap: after a NEGATIVE question ja agrees with the not; doch is the answer then. A comma follows it, then a full statement.

sentences.trap: ja does not join to the sentence behind it. German writes the comma and then a complete statement, exactly as English does — there is no shorter form where the answer swallows the sentence.
sentences.sound: yah, ish HIGH-suh VAY-ber. German j is an English y, every time: ja is "yah", and it never has the sound of English "jam".

variations.changed: the answer flips, and the sentence behind it changes with it
a different verb gives the same answer — sein instead of heißen, and the title comes with it
the same ja frame answering a completely different question

mistake.why: The verb is the SECOND element of a German main clause, so it comes straight after ich: Ja, ich heiße Weber. Sending the verb to the end is something German really does — but only in a subordinate clause, and this is not one.

sentences.usage: Confirming who you are. The comma is real: ja answers, and the sentence that follows it stands on its own feet.
sentences.mnemonic: j is y. Once ja stops looking like an English j it stops looking foreign.

words.note: Three words as one piece: literally “how goes it”. es is an empty subject; the person comes later, in a case slot. It asks how it goes FOR you, not how you are.
The dative of Sie — “to you”. In a wellbeing sentence the person sits in the dative, not the subject slot. Capitalised like Sie and Ihr; lowercase ihnen (“to them”) is not taught.

sentences.trap: English puts the person in the subject slot — "how are YOU". German puts a meaningless es there and drops the person into the dative instead. Build it the English way and you get a sentence with no subject in it at all.
sentences.sound: vee GAYT ess EE-nen. geht has a long "ay" and a silent h — the h is there to stretch the vowel, the same trick you saw in Ihr and Name. The final -t is crisp, and Ihnen begins with that long "ee" again.

variations.changed: the same question about a third person — a name in the dative slot shows no ending at all
drop the question word and the verb takes the front: an open question becomes a yes/no one
the answer, out of the same parts — mir replaces the question word and the person moves to the front

mistake.why: That asks what you are LIKE as a person, not how you are doing. German does not build this question with sein at all — it uses the going-construction, with the person in the dative: Wie geht es Ihnen?

sentences.usage: The greeting that follows the greeting, with anyone you are on Sie terms with. The casual Wie geht's? is the du-flavoured shortening — you will hear it all day long, and this course never writes it, because its register is not the one you want with a stranger.
sentences.mnemonic: Not "how are you" but "how goes it to you". The person is never the subject in this sentence.

words.cue: I am (doing) · things go for me
words.note: The answer to Wie geht es Ihnen?, taken whole: “to-me goes it” — mir is dative “to me”, es the empty subject, gut follows. A SHAPE German reuses: Mir ist kalt, “I'm cold”.
Good — and “well”, where English splits them. After sein and after the going-construction it takes no ending: an adjective only grows endings before a noun.
Thank you — the whole thing, no verb, no pronoun, tacked onto an answer like English “thanks”. The reply is bitte, a word with several later jobs.

sentences.trap: "I am fine" is the English shape and it does not survive the crossing: Ich bin gut means you are good AT things, or a good person. The wellbeing answer keeps the person in the dative — Mir geht es gut.
sentences.sound: meer GAYT ess GOOT, DAN-kuh. mir has the same long "ee" as Ihnen, and gut a long pure oo. danke is two syllables and ends in that unstressed "uh" — never one syllable, never "dank".

variations.changed: drop the thanks — the sentence is already complete without it
the thanks moves to the front instead, and nothing inside the sentence shifts
a name takes the dative slot at the front — the same frame, about somebody else

mistake.why: Not an answer to Wie geht es Ihnen? — it says you are good at something, or a good person. Wellbeing keeps the person in the dative and the subject slot empty: Mir geht es gut.

sentences.usage: The standard reply, in a shop, an office or a corridor. It is short on purpose — nobody asking this wants a report.
sentences.mnemonic: The question is "how goes it to-you" and the answer is "to-me goes it well". Same three words, the person swapped at the front.

words.note: Tired. After sein an adjective takes no ending, as in English: Ich bin müde, Sie sind müde, Anna ist müde. The ü is a letter — write the dots.

sentences.trap: This one is nearly free — English inverts for "be" as well: "are you tired". The delta is that German does exactly the same for EVERY verb it has, and the last card of this rung is where that stops looking like English.
sentences.sound: zint zee MÜ-duh. A single s in front of a vowel is voiced like a z, so both Sind and Sie open with a z sound. A final d hardens to t, so sind ends in a t. For ü: say "ee" and round your lips as if for "oo" without moving your tongue.

variations.changed: a bare noun instead of an adjective in the same verb-first frame — and still no ein in front of the job
the statement the question was made from: the only difference is where sind stands
the question turns negative — and its yes is no longer ja but Doch

mistake.why: There is no German word standing in for English "do". This is not a near miss; it is a sentence with two verbs and no grammar holding them together. The question is made by moving the verb you already have: Sind Sie müde?

sentences.usage: Asked of somebody you are on Sie terms with — a colleague at the end of a shift, a passenger, a patient.
sentences.mnemonic: Statement, then swap: Sie sind müde becomes Sind Sie müde? Nothing is added and nothing is dropped.

words.note: No. It ANSWERS a question and does not negate a sentence — which is why this line says the no twice, once as the answer and once inside the sentence with nicht, exactly as English says "no, I'm not".
The general “not”: it negates a verb, an adjective or a sentence, AFTER the verb or at the end — Ich bin nicht müde. No “do”, no “don't”. A noun that took ein is negated with kein instead.

sentences.trap: English needs "am not" or "don't" and builds the negative out of an auxiliary. German has no auxiliary to build and none to drop: one word, nicht, placed after the verb.
sentences.sound: nine, ish bin nisht MÜ-duh. nein rhymes with English "nine" — ei is always "eye". nicht ends in the same soft front ch as ich, so the two of them rhyme with each other.

variations.display: Nein, ich wohne nicht in Berlin
variations.cue: No, I don't live in Berlin
variations.changed: nicht negating a whole statement instead of an adjective — still straight after the verb
drop the answering nein — the sentence negates itself perfectly well
the person shifts to Sie and nicht does not move an inch

mistake.why: nicht comes AFTER the verb, not in front of it. English's "not" leans on an auxiliary — "do not", "am not" — and German has none to lean on, so the verb keeps its second place and the not follows it: Ich bin nicht müde.

sentences.usage: Turning down an offer, correcting an assumption, answering a question straight.
sentences.mnemonic: Verb first, not second: the verb keeps its place and nicht comes along behind it.

sentences.cue: Yes I am — I am tired

words.note: The yes that CONTRADICTS a negative question — English has no word for it. Sind Sie nicht müde? — ja agrees with the not; Doch means “yes, I am”. It answers a negative statement the same way.

sentences.trap: English's "yes" is ambiguous after a negative question and speakers patch it with "yes I am". German is not ambiguous and does not patch: ja after a negative question agrees with the negative, and doch is the only word that disagrees with it.
sentences.sound: dokh, ish bin MÜ-duh. Doch ends in the rasping back ch of Buch, because the vowel in front of it is a back vowel. Set it against nicht and ich, where the same two letters are the soft front sound — the vowel before the ch is what decides.

variations.cue: Yes I am — I am a student
variations.changed: the same contradicting yes in front of a different sentence

variations.cue: Yes I do — I like coffee
variations.changed: answering a different negative question, "don't you like coffee?" — doch covers English's "yes I do" as well as its "yes I am"
contradicting a negative wellbeing question: Geht es Ihnen nicht gut?

mistake.why: Perfectly good German, and the wrong answer to Sind Sie nicht müde? — after a negative question ja lines up with the not, so it says you are NOT tired. The contradicting yes is Doch.

sentences.usage: Only after a negative question or a negative statement. Asked Sind Sie müde? you answer Ja; asked Sind Sie nicht müde? you answer Doch.
sentences.mnemonic: Doch is the word that shoves back. If there is a not in the question and you disagree with it, doch is the only yes that will do.

words.note: sprechen, “to speak”: ich spreche, Sie sprechen — the Sie form spelled like the infinitive again. A language name follows it BARE: no article, no “in”.
German, the language — a noun, so capitalised, and bare after sprechen: no article, no “in”. The adjective is the same word lowercase; the course teaches only the language name.

sentences.trap: The English question needs "do" and German has nothing to put in that slot. The verb itself goes to the front and that is the entire question: Sprechen Sie Deutsch? Here, unlike Sind Sie müde?, English cannot invert on its own and the gap is finally visible.
sentences.sound: SHPREH-khen zee DOYTCH. An initial sp- is "shp", the same rule that made Student "shtoo-dent". eu is always "oy", so Deutsch begins "doy", and the tsch on the end is the ch of English "watch".

variations.changed: the answer: the -en ending becomes -e for ich, and the verb drops back into second place
the same verb-first frame with a different verb — nothing else about the question changes
a third verb through the same frame: verb, then Sie, then the rest

mistake.why: A language name after sprechen stands bare, with no article: Sprechen Sie Deutsch? The article would make it a particular German, which is not a thing there is.

sentences.usage: The single most useful question in this rung — asked of a stranger before you commit to a conversation in either language.
sentences.mnemonic: Verb, then Sie, then the rest. Sprechen Sie …? is the frame; drop any verb into the front of it.

comprehensionPool.display: Nein, ich wohne nicht in Berlin
comprehensionPool.cue: No, I don't live in Berlin
Do you speak German, Mrs Weber?
You are tired — or: they are tired. At the start of a sentence the capital tells you nothing, and the plural verb fits both.
Yes I am — I am a student
